newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen party slams government over vote count delay.
newsitem.headline: Yemen party slams government over vote count delay.

text.p: Yemen said on Monday it was delaying the announcement of initial results in its first parliamentary elections since a 1994 civil war because high voter turnout had slowed counting.

But outgoing parliament speaker Sheikh Abdullah Bin Hussein Al-Ahmar, whose Islah Party is a junior coalition partner in the government, accused some ruling party members of hampering vote counting in many constituencies.

Al-Ahmar insisted at a news conference in his hometown of Khamir, outside the capital Sanaa, that the announcement of results was delayed because some General Peoples Congress (GPC) members, local officials and candidates wanted counting to be done in military camps instead of designated polling stations.

"The results are late because the GPC is hampering counting in many constituencies," he said. "This is a violation of the law. It is evidence of bad intentions...We will not accept the transfer of ballot boxes."
Al-Ahmar, a key figure in Yemeni politics, gave no further details. Government officials were not available for comment.
Tensions had been simmering in the run-up to the polls between Yemen's ruling GPC party and Islah, an influential Islamist party, diplomats say.

Saeed al-Hekaimi, spokesman for the Supreme Election Committee, said first results would be announced by noon on Tuesday. Yemeni officials had earlier said they expected initial results on Monday afternoon.

Hekaimi said turnout had been high due to new voting cards that carried election symbols for many candidates in Sunday's ballot, which was overshadowed by two fatal shootings in which nine people died.
This encouraged many of Yemen's illiterate voters to take part, swelling turnout which officially was put at 80 percent although international monitors believed it was closer to 60 percent.
Witnesses said Sanaa appeared calm on Monday as military police armed with assault rifles manned polling stations while votes were counted.

Hekaimi said voting would be repeated in a constituency in Dhamar, 100 km (60 miles) south of Sanaa -- scene of some election violence -- after voters refused to cast ballots because the symbol of their candidate was missing due to an administrative error. He gave no new date.

Hekaimi also reported "a new incident of election violence in Dhamar" but declined to elaborate. An election observer told Reuters that three people were wounded, two seriously, after supporters of the Dhamar candidate whose symbol was missing opened fire on a car carrying supporters of his rival.
Before voting began, a soldier opened fire on people at a polling area in the town of Mukayras, killing five soldiers and three civilians, Interior Minister Hussein Mohammad Arab said.
Arab said security officials were investigating the incident but no political motive had been established. He said one of the victims of the first attack was a GPC member.
Also on Sunday, a man refused access to a polling station in Dhamar fired on a security officer who died after the attack.
Election observers said the violence was not surprising as many Yemenis routinely carry Kalashnikov assault rifles and other firearms. Some incidents are related to tribal strife.
One election observer said the voting and counting seemed free of violations in several polling stations visited.
Western diplomats expect President Ali Abdullah Saleh's GPC and Islah to retain power.

The main opposition Yemen Socialist Party, some of whose former leaders launched the separatist campaign that sparked civil war, and three others boycotted the polls due to alleged irregularities. The government denied the charges. 1525 280497 GMT
